A fuel-burning kiln has less available oxygen than the flame requires. The atmosphere draws oxygen from glaze and body compounds. Electric kilns normally oxidise unless they are specifically designed for another atmosphere.
A glaze over another glaze is a new chemical system—not paint mixing. Plan both directions, vary thickness deliberately, and let fired evidence decide.

Judith Laqueur-Révész

Judith Laqueur-Révész worked at every scale: hand-thrown vessels, small ceramic sculptures, sculpted portraits and architectural reliefs. Her ceramics moved beyond the studio into the streets of Amsterdam and onto a villa façade in Italy. Today, her work holds a place in the Nederlands Tegelmuseum.

Judith trained in Budapest with sculptor Márk Vedres before working as a ceramic artist in Amsterdam. Her studio in the Hanedoesstraat, The Hague, is documented in the specialist Capriolus profile. The documentary’s caption points to a photograph of that atelier in the February 1960 issue of Moeder ; the original printed page and photographer have not yet been located. The February 1960 Moeder-Vrouwenpost issue is the next source to inspect for that photograph.

Judith worked with vessels, tableware, small sculpture, portraits and ceramics made for buildings. The records below name works and exhibitions that can be traced. They form the beginning of a catalogue, not a claim that her complete oeuvre has been found.

Judith’s dates are documented by the Capriolus artist profile ↗ . The museum photographs above show documented works; the amphora gallery presents the family collection with its own provenance notes. Made in 1960–61 for the villa L’Elefante Felice in Porto Ercole, Judith’s ceramic elephant occupied its outside wall for more than fifty years. When the villa was demolished in 2012, the relief was saved with part of the wall. Conservators later separated and restored its ceramic elements before mounting them on a new support.

Oxidation, reduction and later reoxidation change copper’s chemical state and the particles that form inside the glaze. Base chemistry, glaze thickness, clay, reduction onset, peak heatwork and cooling all decide whether copper reads green, clear, liver-brown, blush pink or red.

Too little reduction may leave green; excessive or badly timed reduction can muddy or liver the red. Reoxidation and cooling can erase, shift or develop colour. There is no universal schedule.
Use separate firings to compare reduction onset. Keep a green oxidation witness. Change copper or tin only after the atmosphere comparison, never all variables together.
Use witness cones. Log reduction onset and strength, pressure or oxygen reading, kiln position, glaze thickness, clay body, peak heatwork and the whole cooling path.
